blocks.text: Rivers supported agriculture and transport without producing one political form. The Nile linked population, movement and farming along a pronounced axis, creating distinctive conditions for Egyptian integration. Kingship, religion and organization were still necessary to make use of those conditions.

Egyptian continuity did not mean unchanging institutions. Across dynastic change, fragmentation and reconstruction, agriculture, temples, writing and sacred kingship entered new political arrangements. What persisted was a combination of capabilities and memories, not an entirely unchanged state.

blocks.caption: Indus Urban Civilization · Context illustration; historical interpretation is in the text.

blocks.text: Indus cities demonstrate substantial organizational capacity, but surviving material does not establish every feature of political or intellectual life. Urban sophistication cannot replace missing evidence. Unknowns should remain open rather than be filled with models of kingship or religion borrowed from elsewhere.

Early Chinese civilization also requires attention to connections among regions. Cities, ritual and integration in the Yellow River, Yangtze and other areas cannot be reduced to the story of one river. Comparison should examine particular organizational conditions instead of deriving institutions directly from waterways.
